summary:
Students can learn what a heat shield, antenna, or fuel tank does and still struggle to see how those choices affect an entire mission. We built Apogee Flight Academy to make those trade-offs visible and testable.

Players use NASA-sourced destination data to plan a mission, assemble a spacecraft, and fly a challenge shaped by their build. Illustrated parts, short tutorials, and live indicators explain the decisions in plain language. The same design choices that determine whether a spacecraft passes preflight also affect how it performs in play. After a run, the game explains the outcome and suggests a specific change to try.

Automated browser tests cleared all eight missions and reached the rescue ending. The companion Systems Lab extends the exercise to orbits, payloads, power, and communications. Together, they give educators a practical way to ask students to predict a trade-off, test it, and explain what happened.

Project Details

Operation Homecoming gives each player a mission objective and a set of constraints.

[IMAGE ID NOT FOUND title:"The mission map with the Sun, Earth, and the Moon briefing open" ]

They choose illustrated components, see them fitted to the shuttle, and check the design against limits such as mass, budget, fuel, power, and communications.

[IMAGE ID NOT FOUND title:"The rocket builder with nine part categories and the assembled spacecraft" ]

A blocked design identifies the constraint and suggests a fix. Once the spacecraft is ready, its configuration changes the challenge the player flies. On Venus, for example, stronger thermal protection improves survivability while adding mass and cost. The report helps the player decide what to change on the next attempt.

[IMAGE ID NOT FOUND title:"The Moon pre-flight briefing with the objective, controls, and success criteria" ]

Systems Lab applies the same approach to orbital mission planning. Players compare orbital altitude, launcher payload capacity, instrument power consumption, and communications data rates. They can test whether a more capable instrument produces data faster than their spacecraft can transmit it. Brief explanations, visual indicators, and linked science references make these concepts accessible to beginners.

We built the game with HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and Canvas. Node.js packages the campaign as a single playable offline file. We used TypeScript checks and Playwright browser tests to verify the campaign, touch controls, and offline play. The spacecraft ratings and flight physics are simplified for learning. A classroom study would be the next step to measure how well students transfer what they learn to a new mission.
